newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK property speculation "serious issue" - Patten.
newsitem.headline: HK property speculation "serious issue" - Patten.

text.p: Speculation in Hong Kong's booming property market will be a serious matter for the territory's post-handover government and solutions will require a delicate touch, Governor Chris Patten warned on Monday.
"I don't want to say that things are getting out of control but I do agree that it is going to be a serious issue for the (post-handover) government to tackle," Patten told reporters.
With the British territory's handover to Chinese rule just 15 days away, the administration of future leader Tung Chee-hwa has begun to formulate plans to curb property speculation.
On Saturday, a Tung senior aide C.Y. Leung said speculation was rampant in the territory and should be brought under control.
Realtors report that in 1996 most property prices rose by a staggering 20 to 30 percent during the year.
They say the surge so far shows no sign of abating
Patten urged a gentle touch in curbing prices.

"While you want to damp down speculation and any excessive increase in prices, you don't want to do anything which would damage the property market or investors' confidence in the medium and long term. So it is a difficult balance to strike," said Patten, who leaves office at midnight on June 30.
Patten said the government had taken measures to dampen speculation, as in 1994, but he cautioned against doing anything that would hurt the investments of homeowners.

"You have to be very careful that you don't take measures which actually knock the pins, knock the foundations from under the housing market because if that happens you are left with a lot of people suffering from negative equity, which is a much more serious problem than a rise in house prices," he said.
Increasing the supply of land was the most important long-term measure, Patten said.
The government has said 260 hectares of land will be made available for private residential development over the next five years, including 70 hectares for low density luxury housing.
Some Hong Kong property developers have urged the government to increase land supply for luxury residential development, saying a larger supply is the solution to high prices.
Leung, a property surveyor named by Tung to head a committee to map out long-term housing strategy, said on Saturday he had completed a report outlining ideas to curb speculation.
"The state of mind of speculators is much worse now," Leung, a member of Tung's Executive Council, told reporters.
"In the past they would at least keep the flats for a while, but right now some speculators don't even look at the property (before reselling it)."
Leung gave no details of his proposals but said they would not affect long-term investors or genuine home buyers.
